Preface
You are a data scientist for a mid-sized business, in a small group of 3-4 data scientists. You’ve been tasked with creating a report evaluating a scenario for your business. Your colleagues will also be evaluating the same scenario, and your reports will be used in aggregate to determine a consensus (or lack thereof) on the company’s action. The reports will also be used to inform downsizing that is rumored to be coming - you want to ensure your report is better than your peers so that you aren’t as easy to cut.
You may talk to your peers who are assigned the same scenario, but you do not want to collaborate too closely, lest you both become targets of the rumored layoffs.

I’ve scaffolded this report for you to make this process easier - as we talk about different sections of a report in class and read about how to create similar sections, you will practice by writing the equivalent section of your report.

title: Appendix B — Draft: Results
text:
Methods
This analysis uses data from the National Bridge Inventory (“Download NBI ASCII Files - National Bridge Inventory - Bridge Inspection - Safety Inspection - Bridges & Structures - Federal Highway Administration” n.d.), Nebraska Department of Transportation bridge reports (“Bridge - NDOT” n.d.), and Federal Highway Administration traffic data (“Highway Statistics 2023 - Policy Federal Highway Administration” n.d.).
The variables used in this analysis are shown in Table A.1, Table A.2, and Table A.3, including measures of bridge condition, age, traffic, and maintenance.
Only bridges located in the Omaha metropolitan area were included. Bridges with missing structural ratings were excluded.
Bridge condition was measured using deck, superstructure, and substructure ratings, along with the overall sufficiency rating. Bridge age was calculated using the year built. Traffic volume was measured using average daily traffic.
To estimate the probability of failure, bridges with lower sufficiency ratings were considered higher risk. Bridges with sufficiency ratings below 50 were treated as bridges with higher risk. The relationship between bridge age and sufficiency rating was also used to identify patterns of deterioration over time.
To estimate the consequences of failure, traffic volume was used as a measure of impact. Bridges with higher traffic were assumed to have greater consequences if a failure occurred.
Overall bridge risk was estimated using the formula:
Risk = Probability of Failure × Consequences of Failure
Using this approach help identify what bridges may need more monitoring or maintenance then others.

title: Appendix B — Draft: Results
text:
Data Characteristics
The bridge data shows that the average bridge age is about 45 years. Most bridges have sufficiency ratings between 50 and 80, which suggests they are in fair to good condition. However, about 12% of bridges have a sufficiency rating below 50, which indicates poorer condition.
Traffic levels vary across different bridges. Some carry only a few thousand vehicles per day and others carry up to about 40,000 vehicles per day.

title: Appendix B — Draft: Results
text:
Primary Analysis: Probability of Failure
The primary analysis shows that bridges with lower sufficiency ratings have a higher risk of failure. Bridges with ratings below 50 were identified as higher risk structures.
The results also show that older bridges tend to have lower sufficiency ratings. This suggests that the condition of bridges generally declines over time and usage. Most bridges are in acceptable condition, but there is a small group of bridges that fall into lower condition categories and are at high risk.
Older Bridges tend to have lower sufficiency scores. This suggests gradual deterioration over time. Most bridges however, are still in good condition. Some do have lower scores that could lead to a higher risk of problems in their structure.

title: Appendix B — Draft: Results
text:
Secondary Analysis: Consequences of Failure
Traffic data shows that bridges with higher daily traffic would, of course, cause large disruptions if they failed. Bridges carrying up to 40,000 vehicles per day would have the biggest impact on transportation.
Maintenance data from NDOT (“Bridge - NDOT” n.d.) shows that some bridges have planned repairs. That would help reduce short term risk. However, bridges that have both high traffic and low sufficiency ratings represent the highest overall risk.
Bridges that fall into the high risk category are those with both lower sufficiency ratings and high traffic volumes. These bridges are located along major transportation routes such as I-80 and other high traffic passageways in Omaha.
These locations are important for daily travel, so a failure in these areas would cause major disruptions to traffic and be a problem to public safety.

title: Appendix B — Draft: Results
text:
Calculation of Bridge Risk
Overall bridge risk combines the probability of failure and the consequences of failure:
Risk = Probability of Failure × Consequence of Failure
As shown in Figure B.1, bridge condition is used to estimate failure risk, and traffic data is used to estimate the impact of a failure.








flowchart TD
A["Condition"] --> B["Failure"]
C["Traffic"] --> D["Impact"]
B --> E["Risk"]
D --> E








Figure B.1: Shows how bridge risk is calculated using condition and traffic data.




Key Findings

Most bridges in Omaha are in fair to good condition
About 12% of bridges are in poorer condition and may need monitoring or repair
Older bridges tend to have lower sufficiency ratings, showing gradual deterioration
Bridges with high traffic volumes would cause the biggest disruptions if they failed
Bridges with both low ratings and high traffic represent the highest risk







Important



Conclusion
Overall, widespread bridge failure in Omaha is unlikely. However, targeted monitoring and maintenance of lower rated bridges is recommended over the next five years to reduce overall risk.

title: Appendix D — Draft: Executive Summary
text:
This report evaluates the risk of a bridge collapsing in Omaha, Nebraska over the nest five years. The goal of this report is to help the people that make decisions for the city understand the current risks and identify actions that can help reduce those risks.
Data from the National Bridge Inventory, Nebraska Department of Transportation, and federal traffic statistics were used to help analyze bridge condition, age, traffic levels, and planned maintenance. Risk was defined as the mixture of the probability of failure and the consequences if a failure does occur.
The analysis shows that most of the bridges in Omaha are in fair to good condition currently. However, there are a couple of bridges that have lower condition ratings which means they are more at risk. The older bridges were more likely to have slightly lower condition scores, suggesting that deterioration over time is also an important factor.
Traffic data shows that some bridges carry much higher volumes of vehicles then others. So, if one of these high traffic bridges were to fail, it would cause a lot of disruption to the traffic flow and could also hurt people. Bridges that have the lower condition ratings and high traffic levels are the greatest risk.
Overall, the risk of all bridges collapsing is very low in Omaha. However, there are certain bridges that need more attention to prevent problems in the future.

Recommendations

Increase monitoring of older bridges with low condition scores
Start and prioritize repairs for bridges in bad condition
Continue regular inspections/maintenance
Focus more on high traffic bridges where failure would cause greatest impact

Taking these steps will help reduce the chance of bridges failing and also the potential problems that could happen if failure occurs.

title: Appendix C — Draft: Intro/Conclusions
text:
Introduction
Bridge safety has become more of a concern in the United States after some bridges have collapsed in recent years. One of those being the 2022 Pittsburgh bridge collapse (“Maintenance and Oversight Failures Led to 2022 Pittsburgh Bridge Collapse” n.d.). These events have made cities become more aware and pay more attention to how safe their bridges are.
In Omaha, bridges are important for everyday travel, especially on major roads like I-80 and over the Missouri River. If a bridge were to fail, there would be major consequences like serious safety issues, and major traffic problems.
The goal of this report is to estimate the risk of bridge collapse in Omaha over the next five years. This is done by looking at bridge condition, age, traffic levels, and maintenance data. The results are meant to help the city understand where they could be at risk of a bridge collapsing and what can be done to help reduce that risk.


Conclusion
The results show that most bridges in Omaha are in fair to good condition, with about 12% of bridges having lower sufficiency ratings. This means the overall risk of a bridge collapse is low, but there are still some bridges that may need attention.
The data also shows that older bridges tend to have lower condition ratings, and bridges with higher traffic would cause the biggest problems if a failure occurred. Because of this, bridges that are both older and heavily used represent the highest risk.
Based on these findings, the city should focus on monitoring bridges with lower ratings closer, they should prioritize repairs for these structures, and continue regular inspections. These actions would help reduce both the chance of failure and the impact if one occurs.
While more detailed data could improve these estimates in the future, focusing on maintenance and monitoring is the best way to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse in Omaha over the next five years.




“Maintenance and Oversight Failures Led to 2022 Pittsburgh Bridge Collapse.” n.d. https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NR20240221.aspx. Accessed April 17, 2026.
